findings.title: Unpinned remote script piped to sh during image build
findings.whyItBreaks: RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh executes whatever bytes that URL returns today as root inside the build. There is no version pin, checksum, or signature verification, so a compromised or changed upstream (or a MITM/DNS issue, since TLS alone does not attest script content) silently changes the image contents — builds are non-reproducible and arbitrary code runs with full build-time privileges. Additionally curl lacks --fail, so an HTTP 4xx/5xx response body is piped straight into sh instead of aborting the build.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, making failure indistinguishable from empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault is an exported function that calls Load and discards its error (`v, _ := Load(key, m)`). Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key and "" as the value in that case; it also returns "" with nil error when the key exists with an empty value. Every caller of LoadOrDefault is therefore forced to conflate 'key missing' (a failure Load explicitly signals via ErrMissing) with 'key present but empty' — the error signal previously reachable at src/store.go:10 now reaches callers as a plain "" value. As an exported/public API this contract defect ships now regardless of in-repo callers, and the name additionally promises an 'OrDefault' fallback that no parameter provides.

findings.title: Run returns before sends complete; close-after-Run callers panic
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously every `results <- j*2` send happened-before Run returned, so the idiomatic caller pattern `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` combined with `for r := range results` was safe. Now Run spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately, so a caller that closes the channel after Run returns causes `send on closed channel` panics, and a caller that stops ranging when Run returns loses results. The happens-before contract of this exported function is silently broken.

findings.title: Goroutines block forever on send; ctx cancellation ignored on send path
findings.whyItBreaks: Each spawned goroutine performs a bare `results <- j * 2` with no select on ctx.Done(). If the receiver is slow, stops reading early, or the caller cancels ctx, every in-flight goroutine leaks permanently blocked on the send (the sequential version at least applied backpressure to the caller). With N jobs this leaks N goroutines per invocation.

findings.title: OR-ing isAdmin into canDeleteRecord removes tenant isolation and privilege checks
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required BOTH admin AND same-tenant. The new `||` makes the predicate true whenever (a) a non-admin's session.tenantId merely matches the record's tenant — so any user in a tenant can delete any record in that tenant, including records they do not own (ownerId is never consulted), and (b) any admin regardless of tenant — so an admin of tenant A can delete records belonging to tenant B. Both are authorization bypasses on an exported permission predicate; the broken contract is the defect even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Catch-all fallback conflates invalid settings with legitimate defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The new try/catch maps every failure — malformed JSON AND schema-validation throws ('bad theme'/'bad fontSize') — to { ...DEFAULTS }. The only caller, updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22), can no longer distinguish 'stored settings were valid' from 'stored settings were unreadable/invalid': previously parseSettings threw and save() was never called; now updateFontSize proceeds to persist defaults+size, silently discarding the user's stored values (e.g. raw '{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"big"}' previously failed visibly, now writes theme 'light'). The exported parseSettings contract itself also forces every future caller to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: buildReport pairs builtFrom commit with artifacts from unrelated 'verified' ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Before: artifacts came from artifactsAt(commit), the same commit reported in builtFrom. After: builtFrom still reports build.ref(branch), but artifacts come from artifactsAt(build.ref('verified')). Substituting: for any call where branch != 'verified' (the normal case — 'verified' is hardcoded and branch is a parameter), verified resolves to a different commit than commit, so the returned BuildReport claims artifacts were built from `commit` while actually containing artifacts from a different commit. Every consumer of BuildReport misattributes the artifact list to the wrong commit. Additionally, 'verified' is not defined anywhere in this repo (rg 'verified' matches only these two lines), so depending on Build.ref's behavior for unknown refs (interface gives no guarantee), this may also throw or return an empty/garbage ref, turning previously-working buildReport(build, 'main') calls into failures or empty artifact lists.

findings.title: recentEntries no longer applies limit, returns entire list
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes .slice(0, limit), so for any limit > 0 the function returns all entries reversed, violating its own doc promise ('Returns at most `limit` entries') and the parameter's purpose. The only caller, renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9-11), relies on that cap: it allocates new Array<string>(20) and iterates page.length, so with more than 20 entries it writes past the intended page size and returns an oversized, partially filled feed.

findings.title: entry-count header counts stale entries that are no longer rendered
findings.whyItBreaks: The new filter drops stale entries from the rows, but headerLines is still called with entries.length (all entries, including stale). For any input containing a stale entry, the emitted manifest declares `# entry-count: N` while containing only M < N rows, so the header and body contradict each other. Any consumer that reads the declared count to size, validate, or iterate the manifest (the whole point of an entry-count header) will over-read, mis-validate, or reject the file. Example: renderManifest([{path:'a',size:1,stale:false},{path:'b',size:2,stale:true}], opts) emits `# entry-count: 2` with exactly one row.

findings.title: execute() unconditionally throws instead of returning transformed input
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function previously returned input.toUpperCase() for any string; the changed body is `throw new Error("always fails")`, so every invocation of this public entry point throws. Any caller (in-repo or downstream consumer of this exported module) now gets an exception instead of a string result — the core path is unusable and the string-returning signature is unfulfillable.

findings.title: Viewer gate in isEligible blocks the read-only action handle() still dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() (src/handler.ts:23-28) treats eligibility and role-dispatch as separate concerns: it rejects ineligible requests, then gives viewers a dedicated "read-only" outcome at line 25. In the base, an active viewer with attempts<5 was eligible and reached that branch. The added `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` makes isEligible reject every viewer, so handle() now returns "rejected" for all viewers and line 25 is unreachable. The guard correctly rejects the value, but the rejected action (read-only handling) was legitimately approvable on its own — the unchanged dispatch branch proves the system still intends to serve viewers read-only.

findings.title: Payment gate in canProceed blocks saving drafts of unpaid orders
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is shared by submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Adding `order.payment === "paid"` is legitimate for submit, but not for saveDraft: substitution of a normal draft {state:"draft", payment:"missing"} yields old=true→"saved", new=false→"blocked". Users can no longer save a draft before payment exists — the standard draft workflow — even though saving an unpaid draft is approvable on its own.

findings.title: Snapshot files come from 'stable' channel instead of the published channel
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot(repo, channel) returns commit = repo.headCommit(channel) but files = repo.filesAt(stable), where stable is the head of the hardcoded 'stable' channel. For any channel other than 'stable' (e.g. the DEFAULT_CHANNEL 'main'), the snapshot pairs channel X's commit hash with the file listing of stable's commit. Consumers receive internally inconsistent snapshots: the recorded commit does not match the files actually published/attributed to it, so every non-stable publish ships the wrong file set under a misleading commit.

findings.title: New `limit` parameter is ignored; build() always returns 10 items
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature `def build(prefix, limit=10)` promises callers they can cap the number of generated items, but the body never reads `limit`: `max_count = 10` (line 2) and `for i in range(max_count)` (line 4) are unchanged. A caller passing `build('x', limit=3)` still receives 10 items — the promised capping behavior that directly affects the returned data is not implemented, and the failure is silent (no error, just a wrong-length result that callers may slice, size, or persist as if it were honored).

findings.title: parse_positive_int performs no positivity validation despite its name
findings.whyItBreaks: The public function is renamed from read_int to parse_positive_int, promising positive-integer validation, but the body is still `return int(value)` with no check. The in-repo caller charge() (src/validators.py:6) does no validation of its own and relies on this function, so charge('-3') silently returns -300 (a negative charge in cents) instead of rejecting the input; total_cents likewise sums negative charges. Callers trusting the exported name will skip their own validation.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates the caller's DataFrame in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `result = df.copy()` and writes via `df.loc[...]` directly on the argument, then returns it. Any caller that passes a DataFrame it still needs (e.g., to diff old vs new values, retry on failure, or reuse the unmodified frame downstream) will find its data silently overwritten — the old contract guaranteed the input was untouched, and nothing in the signature or name signals the change to in-place mutation.

findings.title: parse_positive_int name promises validation the body does not implement
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER C: the renamed public function promises a positive int, but the body `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` accepts any i64 (e.g. "-5" parses to -5) and maps unparseable input to 0. The caller `charge` (src/parse.rs:6) trusts the result directly: charge("-5") returns -500 (a negative charge) and charge("abc") returns 0, indistinguishable from charge("0"). The new name invites callers to skip their own validation of a promised-but-absent guarantee.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves items; items.len() below is use-after-move (E0382)
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg!(expr) takes its argument by value and returns it; here the return is discarded, so `items` (Vec<String>, not Copy) is moved and dropped at the semicolon on line 2. Line 3 then calls `items.len()` on a moved value — the compiler rejects this with E0382, so the crate fails to build and every downstream consumer of `process` is broken.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against 'latest' but replayed on pinned fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset interface documents (src/changeset.ts:6-8) that fromRevision is the revision 'the changed paths were computed against' and that consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly that revision. The diff resolves the caller-supplied pinnedTag into `from`, reports it as fromRevision, but computes changedPaths from store.resolve("latest") instead of `from`. Whenever pinnedTag and latest resolve to different revisions — the entire reason pinning exists — consumers replay the wrong path set on the pinned revision (paths missing or extra relative to that base), silently corrupting the replay. It also hard-codes the magic tag "latest", which will throw/misbehave on stores without that tag. The unchanged doc contract now promises behavior the body does not implement (TRIGGER C).

findings.title: Rename of users.email leaves src/query.sql selecting a nonexistent column
findings.whyItBreaks: 0001_init.sql creates the column as `email` and src/query.sql:1 is `SELECT email FROM users;`. After this migration runs, the column is `contact_email`, so the existing query fails with an unknown-column error the moment the migration is applied.

findings.title: Hardcoded live API key committed to source
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaces `process.env.BILLING_API_KEY` with a literal `bk_live_...` key. Secrets in source are exposed to anyone with repo access and persist in git history; deployments can no longer rotate or scope the key per environment, and the missing-key guard was removed so misconfiguration is no longer detectable.

findings.title: Inverted admin guard lets non-admins purge projects, blocks admins
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior: purge succeeds only when `user.isAdmin && project.archived`. New behavior: `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden"` rejects the only authorized callers (admins), and the fall-through `db.delete(project.id)` now executes for every NON-admin caller with an archived project. This is an authorization inversion: unprivileged users can permanently delete archived projects (data loss), while the legitimate admin purge path returns "forbidden" (broken workflow).

findings.title: startup() crashes on missing config file after removing None fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() explicitly returns None when the file does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). The deleted guard substituted defaults {'workers': 1, 'region': 'us-east-1'} in that case; now settings is None and settings["workers"] raises TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable, so startup with a missing config file crashes instead of running with default workers.

findings.title: Charge discards Submit error and returns nil on gateway failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` with `log.Printf(...)` and falls through to `return nil`. Every caller of the exported Charge function now receives nil when the payment gateway rejects the submission, so failure is indistinguishable from a successful charge — callers may record, bill, or report the charge as completed. The log line does not restore the error signal at any decision point.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, causing cross-tenant settings leak
findings.whyItBreaks: store.fetch(tenantId, name) is tenant-scoped, but the cache key changed from `${tenantId}:${name}` to `settings:${name}`. After settingsFor('tenantA','theme',store) caches tenantA's value under 'settings:theme', settingsFor('tenantB','theme',store) hits that entry and returns tenantA's setting — tenant B is served another tenant's data indefinitely (until eviction). The changed invalidate(name) compounds it: per-tenant invalidation is now impossible (the tenantId parameter was removed), so there is no way to clear one tenant's entry without clearing everyone's.

findings.title: reserve() oversells last unit: await between stock check and decrement
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, reserve() was fully synchronous, so the read at line 15 (this.stock.get) and the decrement at line 18 (this.stock.set) were atomic within one JS turn. The added `await this.store.save(...)` at line 17 yields to the event loop between check and set. With stock(sku)=1, two concurrent reserve(sku) calls both read remaining=1, both pass the `remaining <= 0` guard, both persist save(sku, 0), both set stock to 0, and both return true — two callers are told they reserved the same final unit (oversell / double booking), while the map no longer reflects that two reservations were granted.

findings.title: Unit change in backoff() leaves retry.ts sleeping 1000x too long
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed its return unit from seconds (Math.min(30, 2**a)) to milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**a * 1000)). poll.ts was updated to drop its *1000, but the other caller, src/jobs/retry.ts:12, still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. sleep() takes ms, so retries now wait 1000x longer: attempt 0 sleeps 1,000,000ms (~16.7min) instead of 1s, and the cap becomes 30,000,000ms (~8.3h) instead of 30s. Any failing job passed to retry() effectively stalls between attempts.

findings.title: Save swallows f.Close() error after switch to defer
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code ended with `return f.Close()`, propagating close-time failures (delayed write-back errors, disk-full at final flush, NFS close errors) to the caller. New code uses `defer f.Close()` and returns only `w.Flush()`'s error, so a failing Close is silently discarded and Save reports success while the data may not be durably written. This is TRIGGER D: an exported function's failure signal is downgraded to a success value; callers can no longer distinguish 'persist failed' from 'persisted'. Save is exported, so the broken contract ships even though the repo has no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_window drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version iterated range(start, end) over the half-open bounds from _window_bounds; the refactor changed it to range(start, end - 1), excluding index end - 1. Every page loses its final row: page_window([a,b,c,d,e], 0, 2) returns [a] instead of [a,b], and a single-row last page (start=4, end=5) returns [] — render_page/summarize then emit output with rows silently missing and gaps in the 1-based numbering.

findings.title: TTL comparison inverted: cache returns expired values, evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: Changed `<` to `>`. Now `Date.now() - entry.storedAt > this.ttlMs` is true only for EXPIRED entries, so get() returns stale values, while fresh entries fall through to `this.entries.delete(key)` and return null. Every get is wrong: hits return expired data, fresh entries are destroyed.

findings.title: pruneDone skips consecutive done jobs and mutates caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: splice(index,1) inside a forward forEach shifts the next element into the just-removed index, but forEach advances to index+1, skipping it: pruneDone([d1,d2,active]) leaves d2 in the result. Additionally the function now mutates the caller's array in place where the old filter returned a new array, so callers retaining the original reference silently lose elements.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores; sort() orders scores as strings
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings, so scores are ordered lexicographically, not numerically. Verified substitution: scores [3, 30, 100], n=2 → sort() yields [100, 3, 30] ("100"<"3"<"30"), reverse() yields [30, 3, 100], cutoff = scores[Math.min(2,3)-1] = 3 → filter keeps all three and slice(0,2) returns the first two players in input order, dropping the actual top scorer (100). Old code sorted [100, 30, 3] with cutoff 30 and correctly kept the 100- and 30-point players. Any score set mixing digit widths (e.g. 9 vs 10) mis-ranks, so topPlayers/formatBoard return wrong leaderboard entries.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison for webhook signature verification
findings.whyItBreaks: Python's == on str short-circuits at the first differing byte, so response time leaks how many leading hex chars of the attacker's guess match the expected HMAC. verify() is the sole auth gate for handle() (app/webhook.py:14), which returns 401 vs executing processor(payload). A remote attacker can iterate byte-by-byte to forge a valid signature without knowing the secret, fully bypassing webhook authentication. hmac.compare_digest exists precisely to prevent this.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transaction after refactor
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version all three statements (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside `with db.transaction():`. The refactor dedented `_apply_balances(db, ...)` so it executes after the transaction block exits and the ledger row is already committed. The debit and credit now run outside any shared transaction: if the credit UPDATE (line 13-16) or the process fails after the debit (line 9-12) succeeds, there is no rollback — the sender is debited, the recipient never credited, and the committed ledger row claims the transfer happened. Ledger and balances permanently disagree; money is destroyed. A crash between the transaction commit and `_apply_balances` leaves the ledger recording a transfer whose balance changes were never applied at all.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time instead of UTC, moving the day boundary
findings.whyItBreaks: Base used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; head uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which depend on the process TZ. The same instant maps to different billing days on hosts with different timezones (e.g. 2024-01-01T00:30:00Z yields "2024-01-01" under UTC but "2023-12-31" in America/Los_Angeles), so billing-day keys become inconsistent across environments and shift for any deployment not pinned to TZ=UTC. sameBillingDay inherits the same drift.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, leaking profiles across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `memo` Map (src/profile.ts:7) is shared across all calls. Changing the key from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account` means two different tenants with the same account name collide: readProfile('tenantB', 'alice') after readProfile('tenantA', 'alice') returns tenantA's cached Profile without ever calling fetchProfile, serving wrong-tenant data (including the wrong `tenant` field on the returned object).

findings.title: load() catch-all converts missing-key error into silent empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff wraps load() in a bare try/catch that discards the 'missing: <key>' error and returns "". Failure is now indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string: loadAll (src/store.ts:12) previously aborted on the first missing key via the propagated throw; it now silently produces arrays containing "" for missing keys, and any caller that persists, reports, or branches on the result cannot tell 'absent' from 'empty'. The catch is also broader than the missing-key case — any future error thrown inside the try is silently defaulted too. load is an exported/public function, so the unusable contract ships now regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Renaming Config.timeoutMs to timeout silently disables the deadline for old callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and timeoutMs is renamed to timeout with no alias or deprecation. Typed TS consumers fail to compile, but any loosely-typed/JS consumer still passing {maxAttempts, timeoutMs} compiles and runs: config.timeout is undefined, so Date.now() + undefined = NaN at src/retry.ts:8, Date.now() > NaN is always false, and the early-return deadline guard at src/retry.ts:10 never fires. The caller's time bound is silently ignored — retry always runs the full maxAttempts, turning a configured timeout into a no-op on upgrade.

findings.title: retryBackground reimplements retry; retries duplicates maxAttempts in one required interface
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is line-for-line identical to the existing retry (src/retry.ts:7) except it loops on config.retries instead of config.maxAttempts. To support it, Config now requires BOTH maxAttempts and retries (src/retry.ts:2-3), but retry ignores retries and retryBackground ignores maxAttempts — callers of either must supply a meaningless second field and can set the two inconsistently. Verified substitution: a caller passing {maxAttempts: 5, retries: 0} hits the guard i < config.retries at src/retry.ts:22 with 0 < 0 = false, so fn is never invoked and the function returns silently — a no-op indistinguishable from success. The retries name also invites off-by-one reading (3 retries after an initial attempt = 4 total, but the loop yields 3).

findings.title: Field input renders length label instead of the value
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the input's defaultValue was the `value` prop itself; now it is always `len=<n>`. Every consumer of Field gets an input pre-filled with a length string instead of the actual value, so editing and submitting the field persists `len=...` rather than user data. This looks like a debug leftover shipped as a regression.

findings.title: value.length is undefined when callers pass a number
findings.whyItBreaks: The prop type was widened to `string | number`, but the body reads `value.length`. For any number value, `.length` is undefined, so the rendered label becomes `len=undefined` — the widened contract admits inputs the body mishandles. This also fails typechecking (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'`).

findings.title: Restore 64MB maxBuffer in git(); default 1MB kills review on large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer reverts spawnSync to Node's default of 1MB (verified: output >1MB sets res.error=ENOBUFS and res.status=null). `git diff mergeBase headSha` (line 140) returns the full PR patch, which routinely exceeds 1MB (lockfile churn, generated files, large PRs). null !== 0 at line 38 throws, the catch at line 182 posts a 'Needlefish: review failed' failure check and sets exitCode 1 — every large PR now fails review. The stderr in the thrown message is empty/truncated, so the real ENOBUFS cause is also hidden. gh() and ghText() (lines 19, 29) kept the 64MB buffer, confirming the removal is not a deliberate policy.

findings.title: Restore `-s read-only` sandbox flag on codex exec invocation
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` against an arbitrary PR repo/prompt with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (src/shared/codex.ts:23). Previously `-s read-only` forced codex's read-only sandbox; without it, codex falls back to its default sandbox (workspace-write or broader per user config), so an LLM agent driven by untrusted PR content can create/modify files and run mutating commands in the reviewer's checkout. This silently removes the only enforcement of the runner's read-only guarantee.

findings.title: Restore merge-base before diffing; raw baseSha gives a two-dot diff
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code diffed merge-base(baseSha, headSha)..headSha — the classic three-dot PR diff showing only head-side changes. New code runs `git diff baseSha HEAD` (two-dot tree diff). When PR_BASE_SHA names a commit that is NOT an ancestor of HEAD — the canonical CI value, `pull_request.base.sha` from the event payload, is stale the moment the base branch advances — the patch includes every base-side change since the real branch point: as reverse hunks (checkout=head) or as PR-authored changes (checkout=merge commit, since GitHub rebuilds the merge ref on base pushes while the payload's base.sha stays stale). changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha) at line 140 shares the same two-dot semantics (line 57), so changedPaths admits files the PR never touched: the reviewer model sees a corrupted patch and inlineComments (line 63) attempts to anchor findings to files outside the PR diff (GitHub rejects those, silently downgraded by the fallback at lines 96-109). Substitution: default path (PR_BASE_SHA unset → baseSha = merge-base(origin/main, HEAD), an ancestor of HEAD) → merge-base(baseSha, headSha)=baseSha and headSha=HEAD, outputs identical, no regression; env path with moved base → patch and changed-files both mis-scoped. The runner's only job is producing this diff, so a wrong diff invalidates the whole review.

findings.title: String replacement in .replace() mangles patches containing $ patterns
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string (not a function) replacement interprets $$, $&, $`, $' and $n as substitution patterns. The previous code used `() => ...` precisely to insert the text literally. bundle.patch is a raw diff and JSON.stringify(bundle) embeds it; diffs routinely contain these sequences (shell `$$`, sed/Perl `$&`, `$'`, Makefiles, regex docs). Any such PR now has its prompt silently corrupted before being sent to the model — e.g. `echo $$` becomes `echo $`, and `$&` expands to the literal `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{PATCH}}` placeholder — degrading or wrong review output with no error surfaced.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently defaults malformed findings instead of rejecting them
findings.whyItBreaks: Every validation throw was removed: invalid severity now coerces to "P1" (line 98), invalid category to "bug" (lines 100-102), missing file to "" (line 103), missing/invalid lineStart/lineEnd to 0 — and Number(raw.lineStart) with a non-numeric value yields NaN with no isFinite guard (lines 104-105). normalizeReview (line 131) previously threw on the first malformed finding in its default strict mode and dropped malformed findings in non-strict mode; it now returns them all as plausible-looking Finding objects. Callers can no longer distinguish 'model produced garbage' from a legitimate finding: a hallucinated entry is persisted/reported/posted as a P1 bug anchored at file "" line 0 (or NaN), and the strict parameter was deleted so no caller can opt back into rejection. This is an exported validation boundary, so the conflation is forced on every consumer of the contract.

findings.title: gh pr view without -R fails on workflow_dispatch before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The Resolve PR refs step runs before actions/checkout (line 42), so the workspace has no git repository on a clean runner. gh resolves the target repo from the local git remote or GH_REPO env; with neither present, `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json ...` errors with 'not a git repository / no GitHub remotes found', the step exits non-zero, and the else-branch (workflow_dispatch, the documented manual trigger) can never resolve head/base SHAs. It only appears to work on a self-hosted runner whose _work directory still holds a leftover checkout from a previous run — fragile incidental state, not a guarantee (fresh runner, cleaned workspace, or renamed workdir all fail).

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed output, yielding a fake empty pass
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously every malformed shape (non-object, missing/wrong-typed summary, findings, checked, residual_risks) threw a descriptive 'malformed review output' error, so the caller could distinguish 'the model returned garbage' from a real review. Now null, {}, or {findings: 'nope'} all coerce to {summary: '', findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: []} — structurally identical to a legitimate finding-free pass. Any verdict computed downstream from this exported parser will report a malformed/failed model run as a clean pass (zero findings, zero blocking residual risks), and the failure signal is unrecoverable at the decision point. normalizeReview is exported and is the trust boundary for raw LLM output; the swallowed-failure contract is the defect itself (TRIGGER D), independent of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Restore PR-ref resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: The job still explicitly supports manual dispatch (workflow_dispatch input pr_number at lines 10-14, job if-condition at line 24, --pr flag at line 47), but the removed 'Resolve PR refs' step was the only thing supplying PR refs when github.event.pull_request is absent. Substituting the new expressions for a dispatch run: line 29 `github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` resolves to github.ref (the default branch, e.g. refs/heads/main), so checkout — which per lines 3-5 provides both the tool code (src/cli.ts) and the reviewed tree — checks out the default branch, not the PR head; lines 45-46 resolve to empty strings, so PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are '' instead of the real base/head SHAs previously obtained via `gh pr view`; line 35 BASE_REF silently falls back to 'main' even if the PR targets another branch. A manual review of PR N therefore installs/runs the default branch's code and reports on PR N with empty or wrong base/head refs.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git(): diffs >1 MiB now fail with ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync without maxBuffer uses Node's 1 MiB default. git() is called at line 100 as `git diff baseSha HEAD` and its stdout becomes `bundle.patch` — the entire input to review(). Real PR diffs routinely exceed 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated code, medium refactors). When output crosses the limit the child is killed, res.status is null, and the `res.status !== 0` check throws `git diff ... failed:` with empty stderr, so the tool's core local-review path hard-fails with a confusing message. The sibling gh() wrapper at line 33-37 still carries maxBuffer 64 MiB, confirming large outputs are an acknowledged case in this file.

findings.title: gh pr diff runs without cwd/--repo, resolving the repo from process.cwd()
findings.whyItBreaks: ghText() spawns gh without a cwd (src/adapters/github.ts:29), and 'gh pr diff' resolves the target repository from the git remotes of the process working directory (gh reads GH_REPO/--repo, not GITHUB_REPOSITORY). Previously the patch came from git(["diff", ...], cwd), which honored the explicit cwd argument. runGithub(cwd, ...) can be invoked from any directory; if process.cwd() is not the checkout, 'gh pr diff' either errors ('no git remote found') or silently diffs the same PR number in a different repository, feeding a wrong patch into review() as the core input.

findings.title: Error-path check conclusion changed failure→neutral, so errored reviews pass required checks
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a 'neutral' check-run conclusion as satisfying required status checks. The catch block fires precisely when review() errored and nothing was verified, and the posted summary even states 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR' — yet the 'Needlefish' check-run now concludes neutral, which a branch-protection rule requiring that check treats as passing. Any repository gating merges on this check-run now merges PRs whose review crashed (fail-open). Previously the same path concluded 'failure', blocking merge. process.exitCode = 1 only helps if the required gate is the workflow job itself, not the posted check-run.

findings.title: Reviewer now runs the PR's own code, defeating the trusted-tool gate
findings.whyItBreaks: The base revision checked out the tool from frankekn/needlefish@main into needlefish/ and only the PR head into target/, with an explicit comment: 'This prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool.' The diff deletes that second checkout and runs ./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts directly from the PR-head checkout (line 59), after pnpm install --frozen-lockfile installs the PR's own lockfile dependencies (lines 49-51). The review step exports GH_TOKEN=secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN (line 56) whose permissions block grants pull-requests: write and checks: write (lines 16-19), on runs-on: self-hosted (line 23). The if guard (line 24) only excludes forks; any same-repo branch PR can therefore modify src/cli.ts (or the lockfile) to always emit a passing review, overwrite its own check result via checks:write, and execute arbitrary PR-controlled code with a write token on a persistent self-hosted runner. The review gate this workflow exists to provide becomes zero-assurance for exactly the PRs it gates.

findings.title: New comment points other repos to a README.md template that does not exist
findings.whyItBreaks: The new header comment (lines 3-5) instructs other repos to 'use the generic template in README.md', but git ls-tree -r HEAD --name-only shows the repository contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json — there is no README.md, so the instruction dead-ends for anyone copying this workflow.

findings.title: Severity parse silently downgrades variants and unknown values to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed String().trim().toUpperCase() normalization means any severity not exactly 'P0'..'P3' — e.g. 'p0', ' P2', 'p1 ' (common in LLM-produced review JSON, which is what normalizeReview parses) — now falls through to the default. Verified by substitution: old code mapped 'p0' -> 'P0'; new code maps 'p0' -> 'P3'. Additionally the fallback itself changed from 'P1' to 'P3', so truly unparseable input (undefined, numbers, garbage) that previously surfaced as a mid-urgency P1 now becomes the lowest, most-ignorable severity. Callers of normalizeReview receive severity:'P3' and cannot distinguish 'producer said P3' from 'producer said p0' or 'producer sent garbage' — a silent downgrade in the fail-open direction for a review pipeline whose findings gate merge verdicts.

findings.title: Restore token scrubbing before spawning codex child process
findings.whyItBreaks: Base deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN from a copy of process.env and passed that scrubbed env to spawnSync. The diff drops both the scrub and the env option, so spawnSync now inherits the parent environment verbatim. runCodex executes the external `codex` CLI whose behavior is driven by a prompt string supplied by the caller; any ambient GitHub credential in the runner's environment is now readable by that agent process (and anything it spawns), enabling unintended authenticated GitHub API use or exfiltration of the token via prompt-influenced behavior. This silently removes a deliberate security control.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard: fork PRs now run untrusted code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only fork guard on a `pull_request` job that runs on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18), checks out the attacker-controlled PR head (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, line 23), then executes it twice: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) runs the forked package.json's root pre/postinstall/prepare lifecycle scripts (frozen-lockfile does not cover scripts; a fork can add `postinstall` without changing the lockfile), and `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) directly executes the fork's own source with `GH_TOKEN` in env (line 33). Any external fork PR now gets arbitrary code execution on Frank's self-hosted runner host: persistence, internal-network access, theft of cached credentials and the runner registration token, and abuse of the write-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN (pull-requests: write, checks: write). The fork GITHUB_TOKEN read-only downgrade does not mitigate the runner-level RCE.

findings.title: readRunnerDurationMs now silently overrides explicit 0ms env config with fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`. Substituting an explicit operator setting: value="0" → trimmed="0" → Number("0")=0 → Number.isFinite(0) is true → `0 > 0` is false → returns fallbackMs. So `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` (consumed at line 124 as the SIGTERM→SIGKILL escalation delay) silently becomes 5000ms instead of immediate escalation, and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` (consumed at line 123 as the post-SIGKILL give-up wait) silently becomes 2000ms instead of not waiting. A zero-length delay is a coherent, previously-working configuration (setTimeout(fn, 0) is well-defined; base code explicitly admitted it), and the misapplication is silent — the operator's env value is discarded with no signal.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop for changed files missing from selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed tail-coverage block guaranteed every changed file got deep-reviewed: files not assigned to a hotspot (or whose hotspot fell outside the MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 slice) were appended as a backstop hotspot. Now the loop at line 97 only reviews sortByRisk(...).slice(0, 6). Any changed file the map pass omits, or whose hotspot ranks below 6, receives zero deep review and nothing in `checked` or the output records the skip — the review reports PASS over files nobody looked at. The deleted comment states the invariant verbatim: 'never silently skip a changed file'.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-pass residual_risks before critic and verdict see them
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D: each deep pass returns residual_risks (including blocks:true entries like 'could not verify X'). The old code accumulated them (`residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)`) and passed them to the critic in candidateMerged, whose output feeds deriveVerdict (line 122) and the returned residualRisks (line 128). The new code hardcodes `residual_risks: []`, so the critic can never see or propagate a deep pass's blocking risk — `[]` is indistinguishable from 'deep passes verified everything'. A review that deep-reviewers explicitly flagged as unverifiable can now produce an unblocked verdict. Confirmed: at HEAD, `res.residual_risks` is read nowhere in reviewLarge (rg shows residual_risks referenced only at 66/72 for small path and 113/122/128 for large).

findings.title: Restore per-hotspot error handling so one deep-pass failure cannot abort review
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted try/catch recorded `DEEP PASS FAILED: <msg>` in checked, pushed a blocks:true residual, and continued with remaining hotspots. Now a single throw from runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview on any hotspot (transient CLI failure, malformed JSON) propagates out of reviewLarge, aborting the entire large-PR review and discarding every other hotspot's completed findings. A 6-hotspot review that previously returned partial results with an explicit blocker now returns nothing.

findings.title: Restore {{FOCUS}} substitution or strip the placeholder from deep.md
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code did .replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)") when building deepPrompt, which is direct evidence that prompts/deep.md carries a {{FOCUS}} placeholder. This PR changes only src/core/review.ts (patchStat: 1 file changed), so the template is not updated in tandem. After the change, every deep-pass prompt contains the literal token {{FOCUS}} and the user-supplied focus never reaches any deep review — a silent steering regression for the large-PR path. The same plumbing removal drops focus/deep from mapBundle (lines 84-89), so focus no longer reaches the map pass either, while the small-PR path still forwards it (reviewSmall serializes the whole bundle at lines 52-56) — behavior now diverges by path size.

findings.title: formatDuration can render "60s"/"Xm 60s" after split rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes by flooring and seconds by independently rounding the sub-minute remainder. When (ms % 60000) / 1000 rounds up to 60 (any ms with remainder >= 59500, e.g. ms=59999 or ms=119500), the rendered output contains a seconds field of 60: ms=119500 → minutes=1, seconds=60 → "1m 60s"; ms=59999 → "60s". The old code rounded total seconds first (59999ms → 60s → "1m 0s"), so a 60 in the seconds position was impossible. The value is rendered verbatim into the markdown stats line at render.ts:75 and render.ts:80, so users see the malformed duration.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0, breaking its public positivity contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns 0. The exported function name and its own error message (`${label} requires a positive integer`, runner.ts:33) promise rejection of non-positive input; callers trusting that contract skip their own check and receive 0 — a sentinel that silently disables or breaks downstream behavior (e.g. a 0 timeout, 0 retry count, or 0 used as a divisor/limit). The error text is also now self-contradictory: "-1" is rejected as not positive while "0" passes. This is a public exported carrier whose promised validation the body no longer implements; the promise affects the data every caller receives.
